Minutes - before Thrive was cool

Born on a drive. Built to thrive.

The idea came on the Tallinn to Tartu drive: ask Scout to turn the group’s shared spreadsheet into an app. About an hour and a half later, the local prototype worked.

On arrival: a local prototype. Firestore, accounts, membership, monthly rounds, offline behaviour and design came later.

Tallinnabout 1½ hoursTartu

From a shared sheet to a shared product.

The sheet already calculated cumulative totals. Awkward mobile editing and editable peer entries made a dedicated app worth building.

Persistent activity, with boundaries.
Firestore holds entries, membership and round state. Logging your activity and administering a group are separate responsibilities.
A continuing challenge, a new monthly round.
The group keeps its identity while each month has its own participants, totals and result.
Membership before participation.
Request to join asks to belong to a challenge. Join enters a monthly round once you belong.
More than a total.
Goals, encouraging messages and friendly competition give the daily logging habit a purpose.

The backbone of the build.

The shared design contract for human and agent work.

One visual language.
Palette, type, spacing, components, themes and motion are written decisions in design.md.
Agreed examples.
Real app styles power cards, calendars and controls. Synthetic onboarding and error states can be explored without touching real accounts.

Project checks keep the guide tied to the build, giving humans and agents a shared reference for new work.

Open the public style guide

Tracking without the tracking hassle.

See where your minutes went.

Totals tell you how much. Categories show what you spent those minutes doing.

Tag it as you log it.
Choose an existing category or type your own when you add minutes. Leave it blank if you just want to log the time.
Look beyond the total.
Switch Your entries to By category for minutes and percentages by activity. Expand a category to see the entries behind it.

From recording minutes to seeing progress.

The sheet already added up minutes. A personal rhythm makes those totals more meaningful.

Count days, not entries.
Start at 3 active days, or choose 1–7. A positive entry makes a date active, counted once across all challenges.
Earn a weekly streak.
Meet your goal in consecutive Monday–Sunday weeks. An unfinished current week does not erase an earlier earned streak.
Keep earlier goals intact.
Changes apply this week onward. Goal history is per name on this device, not Firebase-synced. Daily streaks are explained separately in the app.

Friendly competition found a voice.

The spreadsheet could show a total. Minutes can respond to what that total means right now, with a little cheek rather than a generic cheer.

The easy part needs a Backoffice.

Name approval, challenge membership and admin access are separate decisions.

Name approval
Approve or reject an account’s name claim. Approval binds the account to that name.
Challenge membership
Approve or deny a request to join one challenge. This is a different decision, grouped under its challenge in Backoffice.
People and permissions
Global admins manage the roster and admin access, and can create and manage challenges. Challenge owners manage only their own challenges.

Fixture: one challenge request, no name claims. Name approval is described from source; this preview does not establish deployed authorisation.

Even waiting gets a game.

Name approval needs another person. That waiting screen became a place for an optional little surprise.

Open “Play while you wait” and a Minutes clock card can hop over tally bars. The game is tucked into the approval screen, not the main logging journey.

Try the isolated version here. It uses the current runner’s geometry and rules, without signing in or sending an approval request.

“Minutes survived” is a fictional game score. It never becomes logged activity. Best is kept only in memory for this story visit.

The prototype was fast. The judgement took work.

Offline needs honest rules.
Entries can queue when durable storage is available. Administrative changes require a live connection.
Identity is part of the data.
Names key entries and membership, so a rename is more than a label edit. Local permission checks do not prove deployed authorisation.
The whole journey matters.
Review phone widths, both themes and depths, empty and pending states, offline behaviour and long content. A passing happy-path test is only part of that work.

Later refinements covered navigation and safe areas, cumulative charts, personal results, calendars and loading. Source, generated output and release assets must stay in step.

The agent could build.
The creator still had to judge.

  1. ObserveStart with a real irritation.
  2. DecideLet the prototype reveal the next questions.
  3. ChangeGive precise feedback and a shared design contract.
  4. VerifyTry the complete experience in context.

Scout made the idea tangible before Tartu. Continued human judgement turned it into Minutes.

Sources & boundaries

This is a self-guided project case study, not a claim of a finished production app built in 90 minutes.

“Minutes - before Thrive was cool” is a playful title, not a verified claim about Thrive’s launch chronology. “Tracking without the tracking hassle” refers to reducing the effort of logging minutes, not a claim about privacy or telemetry.

The origin story

The Google Sheet, awkward mobile editing, editable peer entries, motivation needs, Tallinn–Tartu journey and roughly 1½-hour local Scout prototype come from the project creator’s recollection. The sheet already contained cumulative minutes. No trip date, adoption count or time-saving metric is asserted.

What the images show

Current product captures come from the local, synthetic DemoStore preview, with its clock fixed to 5 August 2026. The cover uses Light Soft. The side-by-side home comparison uses Light Pop and Dark Soft, captured from the same screen without changing the person, data or viewport. The challenge uses Light Pop and the calendar uses Dark Soft. Screen names and figures are fixture data, not real people or adoption metrics. They show later development, not the first prototype.

The spreadsheet is an illustrative reconstruction. The style-guide board arranges real rendered H2, typography, palette and component specimens from the current portable guide. Their original assets and app styles are retained; the surrounding layout is composed for the story. The guide has its own synthetic reference states, not the August 5 DemoStore fixtures.

Historical design references

  • workspace/archive/backups/next.backup-preC8-20260830-203540.html: earlier neutral challenge rows, dark indigo chrome, emoji identifiers and the preserved M-clock mark.
  • docs/design.md, lines 63–80: translating Figma inspiration to a phone app.
  • docs/decisions.md, lines 274–307, 475–490, 707–726 and 783–806: selective inspiration, navigation, pastel cards and challenge colour identity.
  • workspace/mocks/figma-direction.html: the “faithful” and “grafted” study directions. Both are studies, not claims of two shipped releases.
  • workspace/mocks/whose-minutes.html: a later clarity study about whose minutes the card shows.

The earlier interface is explicitly reconstructed from preserved styles and layout. The two Figma-direction specimens are sanitised, static re-renderings of the study. Real identities, remote resources and all original scripts were excluded. These are not untouched historical screenshots.

These are relative names in the preserved historical archive. They are not required to open this file. Preserved backup filenames and repository history do not establish the date or appearance of the first 90-minute prototype.

Current implementation evidence

Current app screens, src/styles/foundation.css, the design/brand/h2.svg asset, source structure, browser scenarios and the style guide inform the product and design descriptions.

The development backbone

The current README.md, lines 301–325, describes design.md and the portable guide as the written and visible reference for identity, palette, type, source components, calendars, controls, spacing, themes, depth and states. Its login, onboarding, pending, returning and error examples are synthetic and isolated from authentication and app data.

npm run design:build, also included in the normal build, generates the guide from design/style-guide* through the existing asset bundler and Alpine, without a network or production SDK. tests/style-guide-source.test.mjs checks the embedded current app CSS, H2 vectors, geometry, motion and real calendar templates. tests/browser/style-guide.spec.mjs covers themes, depths, phone widths, inputs, focus, overflow and isolation. These are project checks, not checks running inside the guide or a general automated visual-enforcement system. No measured time saving, eliminated rework or flawless consistency is claimed.

The interactive H2 demonstration uses the generated values in src/app/welcome-motion.js and the transform origin in src/styles/login.css. It retains the product’s artwork, keyframes, 640 ms duration, 160 ms stagger and easing. Reduced motion is the production 160 ms opacity-only fade, with no transform or stagger. The case study adds explicit Play, Replay and Stop controls and cancels playback when hidden. Historical Winding Key motion belongs to Stack, not H2, and is not replayed here.

Progress, motivation and the operational half

README.md, lines 161–183, documents the weekly goal: initially three active days, selectable from one to seven, with positive entries counted once per date across challenges. Weeks are Monday to Sunday. An unfinished current week preserves an earlier earned streak; changed targets apply this week onward. Goal history is per name on this device, not Firebase-synced. The calendar and earned streak shown here use synthetic fixtures.

src/app/motivation.js supplies the three exact message choices. Their illustrative User/Owner totals match the empty-board, tied-leader and 15-minute-lead branches. These are predetermined rule-based phrases, with date-based choice rotation, not generative coaching. The story holds the examples still instead of copying the app’s 12-second Today/month cycle.

src/views/backoffice.html supplies the operational scopes and the distinction between name claims and challenge membership requests. The two Light Pop Backoffice images are navigation-only captures from a fresh synthetic AdminOwner preview. This fixture has a pending challenge request but no pending name claims. No approval, role change, challenge creation or record mutation was submitted.

The waiting-room game

src/app/login.js, lines 326–535, contains the original clock-card runner. The “Play while you wait” disclosure is in the waiting-for-name-approval screen in src/views/login.html. The story isolates its mechanic; it does not include or execute the full login module.

The clock-card geometry comes from WAIT_GAME_GEOMETRY in src/app/welcome-motion.js. The 18-pixel player, jump impulse, gravity, obstacle sizes/gaps, speed progression, collision margin and score divisor are retained. The story keeps the stage visible with explicit Start/Pause controls, Clawpilot colours and instructions. It stops on chapter exit, offscreen playfield or hidden tab and never resumes automatically. Best score stays in memory. No app storage, Firebase, login or approval action is connected.

Logo provenance and status

Five installed-icon SVGs were read directly from icons/icon.svg at verified release commits. No historical app code was executed. Geometry, colours and tile backgrounds are retained; only title punctuation was normalised.

  • 581a373: preserved earlier M-clock installed icon. The import date is not the project’s inception date.
  • 3ede5df: Stack and Winding Key in the login UI while the installed icon remained M-clock. aba3a40: the shipped Stack icon set.
  • 74ccad3: optically refined Stack, with unequal 92 / 100 / 110 proportions and longer 10:10 hands.
  • d34625d: shipped H2 joined-hourglass identity. c5d3497: flatter installed exports and clear-space refinements.

design/logo-directions.json and design/logo-concepts/ preserve the Tally and Monogram alternatives. They are shown as concept branches, not released app identities. H2’s current mark and motion are documented in design.md, lines 500–568, and design/brand/h2.svg.

Selected product turning points

  • f4f9749, f517737, b2c88e2: timeline header, safe areas and scroll/header behaviour.
  • 7efd973, 2536515: cumulative chart, personal results and card geometry.
  • d34625d, 39e0760, 1890b1d, 18de155: activity, entry/calendar, loading and activity-card refinements.

Local evidence has limits. DemoStore replaces the live backend. An isolated Firestore emulator supports local checks; neither it nor the demo proves live Google OAuth or deployed Firestore authorisation. This case study makes no “cheat-proof” security claim.

Offline and asset notes

Minutes is an installable, phone-scale PWA built with vanilla JavaScript and Alpine. App source shares an IIFE scope and builds into generated HTML. Bundled fonts and the offline shell avoid a CDN dependency for the core interface. DemoStore supports isolated previews and a separate Firestore emulator supports local checks. These capabilities came after the first local prototype.

How a nudge gets its context

The rules inspect Today or the selected month: an empty board, zero personal activity, ties, leads, close gaps of 30 minutes or less, and completed-month recaps. The date rotates choices within the written phrase pool. The current app alternates distinct Today/month messages every 12 seconds. The story keeps three examples still for comparison.

The portable story

The HTML contains its own runtime, images and logo artwork. It loads no CDN, analytics, iframe or live product data. Only the explicitly labelled app and style-guide links leave the artifact.
